extracted.intended_audience: public commenters, advocates, and organizers participating in administrative rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what makes a public comment effective during agency rulemaking: what agencies read and respond to, how comments are processed, and tactical tips to increase influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (on-topic + reasoned/new data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must respond to "significant comments" — those that are on-topic and provide "new data and/or specific and reasoned arguments for or against elements of the proposed rule."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies respond to significant comments, focus on being on-topic and providing either new data or specific, reasoned arguments tied to elements of the proposal. The agency evaluates whether comments contain scientific, technical, economic, or legal rationale worth incorporating.

rubrics_metrics.name: New data or analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Present new data or analyses not in the agency's original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing new evidence or analysis strengthens a comment and increases the chance the agency will consider incorporating it into the final rule. This is explicitly listed as a feature that "strengthens your comment."

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, reasoned arguments with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific, reasoned arguments with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue for or against particular elements of the proposed rule with clear reasoning and supporting evidence (scientific, technical, economic, or legal). Vague assertions without rationale are less likely to be treated as significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly label which rule sections you address
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly label which rule sections your points address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies sort and often divide lengthy submissions into parts matched to specific rule sections so that specialists can address relevant comments efficiently. Explicitly indicating the section(s) you are addressing helps reviewers find and use your input.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-topicness and specificity (avoid vague/off-topic material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies "disregard comments they deem off-topic, vague, or otherwise inappropriate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague language and off-topic material. Keep comments focused on the proposal at hand and provide concrete points; otherwise the agency may disregard them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid form-letter effects; individualize and organize submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff and contractors sort comments, grouping form-letter campaigns and dividing lengthy submissions into parts matched to specific rule sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies group form-letter campaigns, individualized, well-organized submissions that are targeted to particular sections and include substantive content are more likely to receive serious consideration than generic or campaign-style form letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide substantive rationale (scientific, technical, economic, or legal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency evaluates whether comments contain scientific, technical, economic, or legal rationale worth incorporating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame arguments in domain-specific terms (e.g., scientific data, technical feasibility, economic impact, legal interpretation) when possible, since agencies look for rationale they can apply in decisionmaking and the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage expectations; combine public comments with other tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: "Final versions of many rules incorporate feedback" from public comments, but "it is quite rare" that rules change fundamentally between proposed and final versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat notice-and-comment as one tool among many. For maximum effect, combine submitted comments with media outreach, litigation, and legislative pressure rather than expecting comments alone to produce fundamental changes.
